name: Yemen
summary: North Yemen became a republic in 1962 and united with the communist South (formerly British Aden) in 1990; a civil war since 2014 caused a severe humanitarian crisis.

location.value: Arabian Peninsula; area 455,503 km²; Sanaa is the constitutional capital and largest city.

terrain.value: High western mountains, the Tihama coastal plain on the Red Sea, the Hadramawt valley and desert in the east.

climate.value: Hot and dry on the coasts and in the desert; the highlands are cooler and get monsoon rains.

resources.value: Some oil and natural gas, fish, and farmland for coffee, qat, fruit and grain; water is scarce.

disasters.value: Droughts and water shortages, floods, cyclones such as Chapala (2015), and cholera outbreaks.

population.value: 32,684,503 (2023 estimate, infobox); the text says 33 million by 2021 estimates.

urbanisation.value: Sana’a is the capital; other cities include Aden, Taiz, Hodeidah and Mukalla, but most people live in rural areas.

disease.value: A cholera outbreak from 2016 became one of the largest recorded; malnutrition is widespread.

migration.value: Millions displaced inside the country by war; many Yemenis work abroad, especially in Saudi Arabia.

economicBase.value: In 2013 services were 61.4% of GDP, industry 30.9% and agriculture 7.7%; petroleum was about 25% of GDP and 63% of government revenue; GDP fell by over 50% after the 2014 war began; in 2019 the UN counted about 24 million people (nearly 75%) in need of aid. Remittances are not covered in the part of the page read.

tradeRoutes.value: Red Sea shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb strait, and the ports of Aden, Hodeidah and Mukalla.

moneyAndTax.value: The Yemeni rial; since 2016 rival central banks in Sana’a and Aden have issued it at different values.

inequality.value: Large gaps between the capital and rural areas.

governmentType.value: A unitary semi-presidential republic under the 1991 constitution. The Presidential Leadership Council has been the internationally recognised authority since April 2022 (seat in Aden), while the Houthi-led Supreme Political Council governs Houthi-held territory including Sanaa.

keyRulers.value: Ali Abdullah Saleh became president of the Yemen Arab Republic in 1978, president of unified Yemen on 22 May 1990, its first directly elected president in 1999, and resigned in 2012. Abdullah al-Sallal is not covered in the part of the page read.

succession.value: Power often changed through coups, assassinations and civil war; Saleh handed over power in 2012 after protests.

institutions.value: A republic with a president, parliament and courts under the 1991 constitution, but split by war since 2014.

stability.value: Repeated civil wars: North Yemen (1962–70), the 1994 war, and the civil war since 2014.

eliteConflict.value: Competition between political parties and leaders.

armyAndTech.value: Rival armed forces: government troops, Houthi forces, southern separatists and tribal militias.

majorWars.value: A 1994 civil war followed an accord signed on 20 February 1994 that could not stop it; in September 2014 an armed movement from the north took the capital, and by 2015 the country was in an ongoing civil war.
majorWars.source: Wikipedia: Yemen (checked 13 Nov 2026); Britannica: Yemen facts and figures (checked 15 Nov 2026) (Britannica confirms the 1994 war ended in defeat for the southern secessionists; it does not cover 2014–15; a named living leader was removed and replaced with a description)

territoryChange.value: The Kingdom of Yemen became the Yemen Arab Republic in 1962; South Yemen was formed on 30 November 1967; the two merged on 22 May 1990 with Saleh as president.

alliancesRivals.value: Houthis backed by Iran; government by Saudi Arabia.

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state.

scienceEducation.value: Literacy is low, especially among women; universities include Sana’a University and the University of Aden.

openness.value: Open to trade and foreign investment, with periods of restriction.

communicationTransport.value: Roads link the main cities; ports at Aden and Hodeidah and airports at Sana’a and Aden, often disrupted by war.

religion.value: About 99.1% Muslim (2020), of whom 65% Sunni and 35% Shia. The Shafi’i and Zaydi shares are not given in the part of the page read.

languageWriting.value: Arabic is the official language; Mehri and Soqotri are spoken by small communities.

artsArchitecture.value: Tower houses of the Old City of Sana’a, the mud-brick high-rise town of Shibam and the old town of Zabid.

socialStructure.value: A largely tribal society, with powerful tribal confederations such as the Hashid and Bakil in the north.

sharedIdentity.value: Disputed: many share a Yemeni identity, but a strong north–south divide remains since unification in 1990.

dailyLife.value: Many families live in stone or mud-brick houses; meals feature saltah stew, and qat chewing is a common social habit.

neighbours.value: Saudi Arabia and Oman by land, and Djibouti, Eritrea and Somalia across the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden.

ideasReligions.value: A Zaydi revival led to the Houthi movement in the 1990s; Arab nationalism and Marxism shaped the 1960s–80s.

riseSignals.value: The revolution of 26 September 1962 ended the Zaydi imamate and created the Yemen Arab Republic.

peakPeriod.value: Too recent to judge; hopes were high after unification in 1990 and the start of oil exports in the late 1980s.

declineSignals.value: None that define the country as a whole.

outcome.value: Still one country, but Houthi-led forces entered Sanaa in September 2014, the government resigned in January 2015, and a Saudi-led coalition intervened on 26 March 2015; the civil war continues.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
